prayer.text: Saint Raphael the Archangel, pray for us.

cues.text: The Healer of God
The name Raphael — Hebrew for God heals — belongs to the third of the three archangels named in the Bible's canonical books.
His entire scriptural appearance unfolds not as a single dramatic visitation, but as a sustained, patient companionship stretched across an entire journey.
Unlike Michael 's sudden interventions or Gabriel 's brief, decisive announcements, Raphael's whole ministry in the Book of Tobit takes the shape of ordinary, extended human friendship.
He walks alongside, advises, and protects, only very slowly revealing the full weight of what has actually been happening all along.
A Guide Sent in Disguise
The Book of Tobit tells of an elderly, devout Israelite named Tobit, struck blind, who sends his son Tobias on a long journey to recover a sum of money owed to him.
Unknown to the family, the young traveling companion they hire — introducing himself only as Azarias , a kinsman — is Raphael himself.
He was sent by God in answer to the prayers of both Tobit and, at the same time, a young woman named Sara.
Sara was tormented in a distant city by a demon that had killed each of her seven previous bridegrooms on their wedding night.
Throughout the journey, Raphael instructs Tobias in small, practical particulars—how to catch and prepare a certain fish, and what its organs are good for.
He offers no hint of anything miraculous, only the quiet, patient counsel of an experienced companion.
Healing Two Households at Once
Following Raphael's instructions, Tobias uses the fish's gall to drive off the demon threatening Sara on their wedding night, and the two are married in safety.
On the journey home, the same fish's gall, applied to his father's eyes exactly as Raphael had directed, restores old Tobit's sight after years of blindness.
Two households, sunk in years of private grief neither had ever connected to the other's, are healed by the same silent guide.

It is a double miracle that Raphael accomplishes not by a single dramatic act, but through ordinary remedies, faithfully explained in advance to those who trusted him enough to follow his instructions exactly.
"I Am the Angel Raphael"
Only after both healings are complete, when Tobit and Tobias attempt to reward their guide with half of everything they now possess, does Raphael finally reveal himself.
He says simply: I am the angel Raphael, one of the seven, who stand before the Lord (Tobit 12:15).
He tells them plainly that throughout the whole journey he had, in fact, been offering their prayers and good deeds before God.
He was present the entire time not merely as a helper, but as an intercessor carrying their own petitions to heaven.
Having revealed himself, Raphael instructs the astonished family to write down all that has happened and to bless God, before he withdraws once more from their sight.
His entire mission was accomplished not in a moment of glory, but across weeks of unremarked, faithful companionship.
Patron of Every Ordinary Journey
The Church has drawn from Tobit's story a devotion to Raphael as guardian of travelers, of the sick in body, and of those seeking a faithful marriage.
These patronages flow directly from the particular graces his story records: safe passage, physical healing, and a marriage rescued from what had seemed a curse without remedy.

Some later commentators have further identified Raphael with the unnamed angel of the Lord who is said, in John's Gospel, to trouble the healing waters of the pool of Bethesda (John 5:4 in some manuscript traditions).
This identification rests on the shared theme of healing rather than on any explicit naming, and is offered by the Church as a fitting association rather than a settled fact.
Legacy
Kept, since the 1969 calendar reform, together with Michael and Gabriel on the shared feast of September 29 .
Raphael's own earlier feast of October 24 has been absorbed into it.

Raphael remains a patron invoked by travelers setting out on a journey, the sick seeking healing, and those who hope, like Tobias and Sara before them, for a marriage delivered from whatever threatens it.
He remains, for every believer who has ever wondered whether their own ordinary troubles were too small to merit heaven's attention, the quiet assurance of his own story.
God's help often walks beside us for a very long time, in the plainest of disguises, before it is ever recognized for what it truly was.
